provenance.note: unverified against silicon. Panel (135x240, ST7789V2), IMU (MPU6886), MCU (ESP32-PICO-V3-02 at up to 240MHz, 8MB flash, 2MB quad PSRAM) and the button GPIOs (A on G37, B on G39, power on G35, power hold on G4) are read off M5Stack's own product documentation. The 520 KB SRAM figure is the ESP32's, from Espressif, not from that page. The power button is declared role power rather than key: the vendor documentation does not state that software may read G35 as an ordinary input, and a silhouette does not get to guess a control into existence. The PSRAM is deliberately absent from the RAM budget: it exists, it is slow, and no firmware here has measured what an app can actually do with it.

unverified against silicon. Panel (1.14 inch IPS, 240x135, ST7789), MCU (ESP32-S2 at 240MHz, 4MB flash, 2MB PSRAM) and the button complement are read off Adafruit's own product page. The 320 KB SRAM figure is the ESP32-S2's, from Espressif, not from that page. ONE button is declared, and that is the point of this silhouette: the board carries exactly two tactile buttons, RESET and BOOT0/D0, and RESET is not readable by an app, so it is not declared at all rather than declared as a control that does nothing. There is no IMU on this board, which is why its sensors array is empty rather than optimistic. Do not confuse this board with the ESP32-S2 Reverse TFT Feather (product 5345), which has three user buttons and would answer a different question.

unverified against silicon. Panel (170x320, ST7789V, 8-bit parallel), MCU (ESP32-S3R8: 16 MB flash, 8 MB OPI PSRAM) and the two tactile buttons (BOOT on GPIO0, the second user button on GPIO14, plus a RESET wired to EN) are read off LILYGO's own repository for this board. The 512 KB SRAM figure is the ESP32-S3's, from Espressif's datasheet, not from that repository. THREE THINGS ARE DERIVED RATHER THAN READ, and are named as derived. The pixel format is the ST7789V's standard 16-bit RGB565 interface; LILYGO's own pages do not state it in those words. RESET is not declared at all rather than declared as a control that does nothing, the same call packs/silhouettes/feather-esp32s2-tft makes. And BOOT is declared as a plain click while GPIO14 is the key: BOOT is sampled by the ROM as a boot strap at power-on, so an app timing a long press on it is asking the board for something it was not wired to promise, where GPIO14 is an ordinary input with nothing else attached to it. The 800 ms long-press threshold on GPIO14 is this descriptor's own choice; no board fact sets it. This is the plain T-Display-S3 and it has NO touch, which is why touch.points is 0: LILYGO sells a separate T-Display-S3-Touch variant with a capacitive digitizer, and that is a different board that would answer a different question.

unverified against silicon. This is a two-part target and both parts are named: the Pimoroni Pico Display Pack 2.0 (2.0 inch IPS, 320x240, ST7789, 65K colours, four tactile buttons and an RGB LED) mounted on a Raspberry Pi Pico 2 (https://www.raspberrypi.com/products/raspberry-pi-pico-2/, RP2350, 4 MB QSPI flash, no PSRAM populated). Panel and buttons come off Pimoroni's own product page and its own driver header (pimoroni-pico, libraries/pico_display_2/pico_display_2.hpp: A on GPIO12, B on GPIO13, X on GPIO14, Y on GPIO15, RGB LED on GPIO6/7/8). The 520 KB SRAM figure is the RP2350's, from Raspberry Pi's datasheet, not from Pimoroni. THREE THINGS ARE DERIVED RATHER THAN READ. The A/B/X/Y labels are the names Pimoroni's own firmware uses; the product page text does not spell the silkscreen out. The pixel format is the ST7789's standard 16-bit RGB565 interface, which is what "65K colours" describes, not a phrase Pimoroni uses. And the roles are this descriptor's own split: all four buttons are ordinary GPIOs pulled up, so any of them could be timed, and declaring A as the key with an 800 ms threshold while B, X and Y stay plain clicks is a choice made here, not a board fact. The RGB LED is real and is not declared, because emu_device() has no output a host could draw for it and inventing one would be describing this file rather than the board. There is no touch on this pack, and no IMU anywhere in this stack, which is why touch.points is 0 and sensors is empty rather than optimistic.

unverified against silicon. Panel (200x200 e-paper, Good Display GDEY0154D67 on current boards and GDEH0154D67 on earlier ones, SSD1681 controller), the four buttons (v2 hardware: MENU on GPIO26, BACK on GPIO25, UP on GPIO35, DOWN on GPIO4; v3 moves them to GPIO7/6/0/8), the accelerometer (Bosch BMA423) and the MCU (ESP32-PICO-D4 through v2, ESP32-S3FN8 on v3) are read off SQFMI's own hardware documentation and its firmware's src/config.h. The 520 KB SRAM figure is the ESP32-PICO-D4's, from Espressif, not from SQFMI, and this file describes the v2 board rather than the v3 because that is the one whose numbers are stated in both places. The refresh timings are Good Display's panel specification (https://www.good-display.com/product/388.html); SQFMI publishes no refresh figure of its own, and nothing here has measured one. FOUR THINGS ARE DERIVED RATHER THAN READ. The format is called mono1 because Watchy's own firmware drives this panel one bit per pixel through GxEPD2; the panel itself is specified with some greyscale capability, so this describes how the board is used rather than the outer limit of the glass. All four buttons are declared as plain clicks and none as a key: they are ordinary GPIOs, but the documented behaviour is a momentary press and a level-triggered wake from deep sleep, and nothing SQFMI publishes promises a short-versus-long verdict, so declaring one would be inventing a control. A device with no key at all is a real answer, and an app that wants one is told so rather than handed a substitute. The BMA423 reports a continuous acceleration vector, which is what that part does; SQFMI's own docs do not describe the output in those words. And the button edges and positions here place four corner buttons on two edges for a host to draw, which is a simplification of a square case with one button at each corner.
